utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you will allow me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner, the witness wanted to say something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'm going to take him through the document in a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Could that document be marked for ID?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Can we have a number for it, for identification purposes only.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. It's P47 ter ID.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, could you describe the document, please. Describe it to the Court, tell us what it's about. Where the -- describe the document first, and then I'll ask you a few more questions about it.

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a document which confirms that I, as is stated here, Dagovic, Esad, was detained in a camp in Bosanski Samac where I was registered on the 13th of May, 1992 in prison in Bosanski Samac. It also says that I was regularly visited from the 13th of May, 1992 until the 5th of November, 1992. I was released on the 5th of November, and this document was issued to me on the 8th of December in Zagreb, which basically denies that I left Orasje in 1994, because Zagreb is located in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. Sir, if the usher could move the document down, and we could see -- and could you show the Court where it's dated, please.

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The document was issued to me on the 8th of December, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And where was it issued to you?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The document was issued to me in Zagreb by the International Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And what have you done with that document since that date? Has it been in your possession, or ...?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The document was in my possession the whole time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And that handwriting above the date, it looks like January 5th, I think, 1994. Whose handwriting is that -- first, whose handwriting is that? It looks like pencil marking.

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is my handwriting. I wrote this now, during the break, because we heard here that I had stated in my previous statement that I had left Orasje on the 5th of January, 1994, which is absurd because I was issued this certificate on the 8th of December, 1992, which is two years prior to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner, I wonder whether actually it could go back on the ELMO for one second.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: And I'm interested in the lower part with the little boxes. On the left-hand side, "was released on 5th of November, 1992," and then we have three possibilities. And if my eyesight is correct, is there a mark in the middle box?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: That's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Maybe you could ask the witness that question, and also what it means, "according to the authorities versus ICRC auspices or according to a/m person." Just for the sake of clarity. I'm uncertain as to what that means.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Do you see the portion of the letter or the document that Judge Williams is referring to, Mr. Dagovic?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: There are three boxes. Box number 1 says: "under the ICRC auspices." Box number 2 says: "According to the authorities." And box number 3 says: "According to a/m person." Are any of those three boxes X'ed or checked off?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The one saying, "according to the authorities."

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. Do you know the reason that that box was checked off, sir?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And what is the reason that it was checked off?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if we look at this text, we'll see that this applies to the situation. So it can be either a case where a person is released under the ICRC auspices, it could apply to a person who was registered in the camp. So if somebody was in the camp and was not exchanged, then this item would apply. The other item, according to the authorities, means that based on what the authorities, or rather, the International Red Cross, said, this is the situation. And the third item applies to a case where this would be issued based on the statement of the person in question. So that would be a third situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner, I'm not exactly clear that I understand the second and third possibilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: At this point, Your Honour, I can see if we can get some sort of clarification. I could only speculate as to what some of these means -- some of these different options concern. I probably have some different views than he would have and -- but I will see what I could -- I'll see what we can do on this matter. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner, I know it's just been marked for identification, but as our usual practice is, it's to be kept by the registry staff. Does he need it? Because then we can just get a photostat copy, because we have all seen the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Mr. Dagovic, do you need that document, or would a copy be sufficient, or do you need the original and we'll keep a copy? What is you preference, sir?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have an original as well. This is a copy. You can keep the copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you. One moment, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, you're in Zagreb, and what do you do next? You go see the Red Cross in Zagreb in January. What's your next step?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First I went to my friend's in Krusevica in Slavonia. I spent a certain period of time there. Then through my friend, I found out that certificates were being issued in Zagreb, so I went there, and I got a certificate. After that, I went to Istria, where I worked, and where I was registered, and I regularly collected my aid payments, the aid that was provided for refugees. And I have the originals of all of those documents, but they're at home. So I could obtain them by tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And what was the time period that -- actually, first, who were you receiving aid payments from, from what government?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the Croatian authorities in Croatia, i.e., from Caritas.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, how long were you receiving aid from the Croatian government?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It went on until I left for the Netherlands. So it lasted throughout 1993. Until the end of 1993, because by 1994, I had left for the Netherlands.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Who were you doing during the year 1993?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I worked in a bar in Istria in Novi Grad, as a waiter.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And during what time period did you work? Did you work the whole year, or a portion of the year?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I worked the whole year.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Do you have any payslips or documentation indicating that you worked that year at this certain bar in Istria -- I'm sorry, in Novi Grad?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't. But I could obtain it. I could call the owner of that bar, if he still has those documents - and I believe that he probably does - so I could get them for you fairly quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, these documents that you have, the -- let's go back to the other one, the refugee aid payments. Do they indicate any address or place you were living at the time?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was Buraj 4 in Novi Grad, i.e. Alto camp Marida. That was where I was registered.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And how long were you living at that address?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I lived there until the end of 1993, until -- right up until I left for Holland.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, what is your current immigration status?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have Dutch citizenship.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Is that based on asylum?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What is the basis?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The basis is three years of continuous residence in the Netherlands.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And are you currently working?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And how long have you been a working resident?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since 1995, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, these papers that you have relating to the aid that you received, where are they?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are at my house.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And are they in some certain location that you could get them here, to this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And when could you have them here?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you would like a copy, you could obtain them this evening. But if you needed originals, then I would need one or two days for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this point I have no further questions. However, I wouldn't mind having the witness produce those documents, since we do have -- since this is a search for the truth, I think he should have the opportunity to provide those documents and see what it says that -- relating to the aid that he was receiving at a certain address within Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. There's no problem. It's up to the Prosecution to arrange with the witness when he can be available to produce them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And I think it would be helpful also that he produces them and also be present again in the courtroom to hand them in and explain them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So even though, at least at this point of the re-direct examination, I'm completed, I wouldn't mind the opportunity just to finish, if it would be five minutes, in having him produce these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. That can be arranged with the witness. I see Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I just wanted, first of all, to object. But then I also would like now to add something to what the Prosecutor said. I believe that if the witness will provide the evidence, as -- in the same way that he provided this document a little while ago, I would like to have the Defence -- for the Defence to receive permission to cross-examine based on these documents. So perhaps it would be possible to receive the documents several days before so that we could prepare and carry out cross-examination on those documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. There is nothing to stop the Defence raising questions as a result of the production of the documents in question. And for your request that they be given to you a few days so that you can -- I'm sure that can be arranged with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. We'd have no objection. It's just at this point trying to obtain the documents and taking a look at them and seeing what we have there. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, all right. All right. Mr. Dagovic, you've heard the exchange that the Prosecution is of the view that they would wish the documents discussed to be produced. And since you were not warned in advance, you didn't have them -- you don't have them with you. So it will be up to you and the Prosecution, through the Victims and Witnesses Unit, to discuss when the documents can be available. And Mr. Weiner, you remember sufficient notice to the Defence, also.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sorry. Your Honour, would you like me to speak to this witness this evening, or do you want to leave it totally through the Victims and Witnesses Unit to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Since you have finished your re-examination and the next batch will be on the documents that the witness is expected to produce, I may as well ask the Defence whether they have any objection to your contacts with the witness as from now on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Those would be limited to getting the documents here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: We don't have no objection, Your Honour. We don't have an objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. The contacts will be limited to the production of the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I intended to do, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. So Mr. Dagovic, you are released for now, but we will expect you to come back and discuss the documents that you are required to produce.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may be permitted to say, since you promised me that I would have the opportunity to say something, and I -- because I wasn't in contact with the Prosecution, I have a couple more very good documents which have been discussed during this examination. I even have a tape recording. So if you would permit me to submit that, or for us to listen to that all together here. I also have my military booklet where my vez [phoen] is stated and where it states where I was supposed to report. I also have a payment slip which would show you what the document looks like when you receive money. And this recording, this audiotape, has to do with the payment or salaries for people. It's about -- a person is mentioned here who was discussed yesterday who was on the payroll of the workers of the hospital. So I would like to submit these documents and listen to them together, perhaps, if the Court will allow that. I would also like to state -- I would also like to state the dates that we discussed here about the dates of my trial in Bijeljina, after my exchange. If we look at it carefully, the gentleman didn't know where and when I was exchanged, so that they are talking about a month earlier in Bosanski Samac. In fact, I was exchanged one month later in Dragalic, in Croatia, which obviously shows that these documents were either made later. But it does indicate that something is not right here in relation to the documents showing where and when I was exchanged. Also, I wanted to ask something, whether these gentlemen also had access to my medical records, my physician records. And if they hadn't, perhaps I could provide them for them, because they were made by Dutch doctors, by a Dutch panel of doctors, and they clearly showed the consequences that I'm suffering from as a result of my detention in the camp. And if these gentlemen are convicted, I intend to sue for damages. Another thing: The apology that I received by the Defence of Mr. Simo Zaric, I do not accept it, because at that time I needed assistance, and I do not need this apology now. And I would like to -- I don't need anybody's pity. I also have a CD with all of the photographs, and I can also submit that. The CD contains some 20 photographs, and they are very interesting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Witness, this is a criminal trial, and in every criminal trial, the evidence is usually limited to only that which is relevant to the indictment. So the Prosecution have elicited the evidence they wanted from you, and the Defence have cross-examined. We are only remaining with one part which the Prosecution wants to complete, and that is the production of documents which indicate where you were during your release or after your release. And that is all that the next stage is limited to. You can discuss with your advisors in the Witnesses and Victims Unit, for instance, but as far as the Prosecution is concerned, their contact with you will only be limited as to what has been stated before. So any other evidence that you think may be relevant, you can discuss with your advisors in the Victims and Witnesses Unit. It will be up to them to discuss with the Prosecution and see whether or not there is need for that to be produced. So for you, you are free to go. And we thank you very much for assisting the Tribunal, but we will still require your presence as indicated.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you wanted to say something?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. At the break, I spoke with my colleagues from the Prosecution, and we have one document which was not admitted. It only received the ID numbers for them. These are the two statements that the witness provided to the SUP. These are the D28/3 and D29/3. When we questioned this witness, we provided the original B/C/S statement as well as the English translation, so there is no reason why these documents should now not be admitted and -- into evidence and be given numbers, because we had these documents be given ID numbers so that this -- they could be admitted through this witness and that he could answer questions about the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weiner, D28/3 and D29/3.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we have no objection to these documents being admitted. However, we're not conceding that they are truthful. We are allowing them to be admitted for what the testimony basically concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: We're not making any statement indicating the truthfulness of those statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right. So they will be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: And I'm sure they will retain the same numbers, but let's just have confirmation from the registry.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. They will be Exhibits D28/3 ter and D28/3, and D29/3 ter and D29/3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have two other suggestions Your Honours. During the break that we just had -- the one-week break that we had, I managed through my investigator to obtain the original statement by Witness M, which was given at the SUP in Bosanski Samac on the 9th of November, 1992. And if you remember, we need this statement because the -- the witness is questioning the authenticity of his signature. This is document D22/3 and D22/3 ID, so I would like now to have admitted the original statement of that witness into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Any objection, Mr. Weiner? Yes, Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honour please, may I just find the document first? I'm trying to find a copy of it. It's taken me somewhat by surprise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And while we're waiting for my learned friend, in the meantime, I have received three official translations of documents D17, D25/3, and D26/3, which were only so far given in the B/C/S version. So perhaps we could use this time to admit those documents as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: You said D17, and then D25/3 and D26/3?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours. And D17/3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: And was the reason for non-admission only that they didn't have English translation?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we were just waiting for the English translation. They are two exchange lists and also the decision to initiate proceedings against Defence Witness L, which we analysed together with him but we didn't have the official translation at that time. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: I think that there probably won't be a problem with these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Which ones? MR. DI FAZIO: The ones that have been raised by my colleague Mr. Lukic. But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No, I mean the first batch or the -- all of them? MR. DI FAZIO: All of them. I -- if my learned friend is able to point out which particular documents he wants to deal with and conduct this exercise with and gives us some time, we can quickly have a look at that, check the transcript, give us -- and provide the Chamber with a clear, coherent picture of our position. At the moment, I'm taken somewhat by surprise, and I -- I don't quite know how to respond without having an opportunity to check the transcript. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Then there's no harm in you being given an opportunity to check, to go back. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you. If we could do that, and perhaps if we could provide a response, say tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Later. MR. DI FAZIO: Tomorrow, I'm sure we could make our position absolutely clear tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. And I recall other Defence counsel, especially I think Mr. Zecevic, saying he, too, had received the translations for various documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. If I may, with all due respect, I have informed the Prosecutors about the existence of the translation. Already ten days ago, I gave them the copies of official translation. I offered this into the evidence. They said they should need some time to check it out. It was Wednesday or Thursday last week, as far as I remember. If they're not ready now to respond to that, I wonder -- I didn't raise the question because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It sounds an appropriate moment because my colleague has already raised this issue about the documents. So whether my learned colleagues can give us an estimation, whether they are prepared now to, I don't know, express their views on these documents or are reserving their time for some later -- later time in these proceedings. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes. Would tomorrow at 2.15 be appropriate? Would that cause too much inconvenience to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: For all of them? MR. DI FAZIO: For all of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. The ones discussed by Mr. Lukic right now and the once given to you already by Mr. Zecevic? MR. DI FAZIO: By Mr. Zecevic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If I may be of assistance, it refers to the documents D22 A to I/2 ter ID. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zecevic. Yes, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, allow me to address this issue also, because it's a part of this general issue that we are dealing just right now. In fact, this morning, the Defence were provided with the -- well, I would say significant number of various documents by Prosecution. In spite of all -- I'm speaking on behalf of myself and my relation with the -- my learned colleague from the Prosecution. In spite of all my efforts on the collegial basis between the Defence and the Prosecution, I think -- it seems to me that something is going wrong. In fact, they provided us with the number of documents only in English translation, which inevitably goes to the -- to the merit. In shortly, that means that they are in possession of certain documents on B/C/S language, and we cannot find it here. It also relates to certain number of witnesses -- witness statement. Also in English without -- without B/C/S language. I would like to remind my learned friends that it's an obligation towards our clients, they have to be supplied with witness statement in their own language that they can understand. And also, the practice that we now -- today is 18 of February, 2002 -- that now they try to discover us, and practically they deliver a certain number of witness statements from 1999, 1998, and all other things. I mean, this practice is a little bit, I don't know, confusing me, because I don't know where is the end of this, I would say, in-trial discovery process.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: They are not -- they are not provided to you under Rule 68 because Rule 68 gives the Prosecution a continuing obligation, whenever they come across any documents they think may be exculpatory, they are obliged to disclose them to the Defence at all stages, because that's continuing obligation. So I'm wondering which Rule --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, that would be very good for us, but I don't see that these are exculpatory documents, especially certain of witness statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Well, no. That is not up to you to agree with them. They may have their own opinion on what they think of a document. So if they think anything in it may be exculpatory -- but because you know the defence of your client and you may not find them exculpatory, but I'm only concerned with Rule 68.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. Frankly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Unless you show that it's not under Rule 68.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. And also the main problem is that, in fact, we don't have this B/C/S version of documents and statements, so I kindly ask this Trial Chamber to take a note about this practice and I hope that our learned friends will try to resolve this problem. It was not my intention to take the precious time of this trial proceedings, but I was -- I was -- in fact, I was obliged to bring this practice, because -- I mean, as I said, in spite of all our efforts to clarify this relation, still --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. But I did say, Mr. Pantelic, I asked you, are these Rule 68 documents or not? When they were giving them to you, what did they say to you?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: No, no. Your Honour. I don't see any reference to Rule 68 here. No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right. Maybe I can hear from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Of course. That would be good, yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think I would save the Court some time in going into the details of what every single one of those documents are. But no, there are no Rule 68 documents included in those documents that were disclosed to the Defence counsel or were available Friday evening and some today. The documents are disclosed because three Defence counsel have invoked reciprocal disclosure, and as the Rules indicate that whenever we come across something that could -- that should be disclosed, we do. We disclose it simply because it's related to Bosanski Samac, not because it's a Rule 68 material. Mr. Pantelic is not entitled to any of those documents that were disclosed here today because he has not invoked reciprocal discovery. Out of a matter of courtesy, we copy him on every document that is disclosed to his co-counsel under their entitlement to reciprocal disclosure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: You don't mean to his co-counsel; you mean to the other three Defence counsel for the other three accused.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: That's exactly what I mean, Your Honours. For Mr. Milan Simic, Mr. Simo Zaric, Mr. Miroslav Tadic, and they invoked reciprocal discovery. And said every time that a document appears in the system -- most of these documents, what happened, in fact, is there's a new collection in Cyrillic in the OTP. We have been searching them. As Mr. Pantelic says, he doesn't have something in English. Most of them we've disclosed in B/C/S without any statement because we consider it may be relevant and we don't want to hold on to the documents until we have a translation. The other statements to which Mr. Pantelic refers are informal witness notes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: So then if you say he hasn't invoked the procedure, then why are we discussing him? All you needed to say is not supposed to receive these documents and he should ignore them because he hasn't invoked the reciprocal --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please pause.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Sorry to the interpreters. We are speaking too fast.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, very shortly, if I may, concerning the same question. I have already raised this issue this afternoon, and I think it would be of assistance to this Trial Chamber that we have agreed, Mr. Gramsci Di Fazio and myself, that we will go over these documents which have been disclosed to us this morning and then he will try to solve this situation and inform accordingly the Trial Chamber. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Then we don't have to deal with Mr. Pantelic on these documents because, as you said, he's not in the procedure that the others have invoked.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you. It is, of course, the Prosecution's position that we oppose the Defence request. And we do so essentially on two grounds: One that the Defence themselves have not established any grounds why this Trial Chamber should exercise its discretion in granting their request, which on any reading of normal procedure is -- would be an extraordinary measure in the normal proceedings. And secondly, it is unnecessary for this Trial Chamber to call the witnesses proposed in order to address the task in front of them, which is the admissibility of document Variant A/Variant B. The Defence request, which was initially put on the record on the 12th of February was phrased as follows. And Defence counsel for Milan Simic said that: "I was hoping that Mr. O'Donnell would not testify to that, trying to interpret a document, because now I have to make a request. All we are going to have to ask for now is the opportunity to get this witness who prepared this letter from the SDS to complete all the information with respect to these documents before the Trial Chamber can make a determination on admissibility." With respect to having reread that transcript and try to ascertain the basis of the Defence request, it is somewhat vague, and we are responding on the basis that the Defence is in fact requesting the Trial Chamber to make either one of the following three decisions: One, to permit the Defence to call its own witness midway through the Prosecution case. Secondly, that it's asking the Trial Chamber to exercise its power under Rule 89(E) to request even further evidence on authenticity of document P3 ID. Or the third interpretation of the request could be that it is asking the Trial Chamber to invoke completely a voir dire process. On any of those processes that the Defence is actually seeking, the Prosecution would oppose the request. And, as I said, above all we reject the idea that any of those measures would be necessary in order for the Trial Chamber to make a determination on admissibility. First, the Prosecution would submit that whichever interpretation of the Defence request is correct, it is clear that they are -- the requests are an exception to the normal proceedings and that therefore the Defence is in effect asking the Chamber to exercise its discretion in favour of the Defence. And it therefore follows that the burden must lie with the Defence to provide the grounds why this Bench should exercise its discretion as requested. And Your Honour, they have not discharged that burden. And I turn again to what the Defence submitted as the reasons for being necessary to call the witness. And perhaps for the record and for the assistance of those in the Chamber today, that was at line -- at page 5741 of the proceedings on the 12th of February, at line 23. And the asserted reason as to why this witness is to be called is because Mr. O'Donnell tried to interpret document 23 -- Defence Exhibit 23/1. Your Honours, first asking a witness to interpret a document does not provide a ground in and of itself for requesting that the Chamber permit a Defence witness to be called halfway through the Prosecution case or, indeed, nor does it provide a ground to move to a voir dire procedure. The Defence has simply not explained why asking a witness to interpret a document should permit them to ask the Chamber to call a witness. Secondly, even if that were -- even if there were grounds for calling a witness on the basis that a witness had interpreted a document, in this case, it's respectfully submitted that the Defence are wrong on the facts. The witness did not try to interpret the document, as Defence counsel themselves went to great length to make clear to the Bench. The witness testified about the document only because Defence counsel considered it necessary to its cross-examination and because Defence counsel sought to have it admitted into evidence. And --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please slow down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Please do slow down for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. And the document does indeed bear a Defence exhibit number. When the witness was originally asked to comment on this document, indeed on the provocative final sentence, it was by Defence counsel. The Prosecution objected, and the Defence counsel argued that this was not an interpretation of the document, but the witness was being asked to provide his professional opinion based on his background. The question in redirect which triggered the Defence counsel for Milan Simic to request the witness was no more an interpretation of the document than the original answer to the question posed by Defence counsel for Blagoje Simic. Your Honours, even when you examine closely the response of Mr. O'Donnell, which again from the transcript appears to be the trigger for the request, there is nothing in that response which, with respect, the Prosecution can find merits granting the Defence a right to call a Defence witness midway through the Prosecution case. He simply testified that the document was referred to in other documents located across Bosnia, that one document had been found by the international stabilisation force. He referred to the fact that some documents which cross-refer to Variant A and Variant B were obtained from the Bosnian Serb authorities, and he referred to the fact that Mr. Karadzic himself had made a clear reference to the Variant A and B at the time that he was president of the SDS. Each of those points he testified in his answer were a statement of fact and indeed covered ground on which Mr. O'Donnell had already testified. So Your Honours, with respect, even on the Defence's own submissions, there is nothing so far in the testimony or the evidence before this Trial Chamber which grounds or goes to substantiate the reason for their request. I would, however, now like to turn to whether or not there are other reasons beyond those stated by the Defence as to why the Bench may wish indeed to call either the witness named by Milan Simic's counsel on the 12th of February or any of the five witnesses who Mr. Blagoje Simic's counsel referred to on Thursday. And with respect, Your Honours, the Prosecution's position is simply that there are no other reasons to call any of the suggested witnesses at this stage. And the reason for that is simply that the issue before the Bench at the moment is one of determining admissibility of this document. And whether the document should be admitted into evidence or not is something to be determined pursuant to Rule 89 and the Rules set out in that Rule, or whether through any reason according to Rule 95 why the document -- or the inadmissibility of the document should be precluded. The rules of inadmissibility are very, very clear and have been pronounced on a number of times by various Trial Chambers and on more than one occasion by the Appeals Chamber. The Prosecution has to establish relevancy and probity in accordance with Rule 89(C), and in establishing relevancy, we have to prove that there is an indicia of reliability of the document. The Prosecution's position is that we have done so. And if the Defence at some later stage wish to challenge the Prosecution's evidence, they can, of course, do that. The question, Your Honour, is when should they be permitted to do that. And that arises when the Defence have the time to present their case. If the Defence want to argue before the Bench the weight to be given to this document, then they can do that and they should do it in the Defence case and in their submissions. They cannot -- it is not the time now to be arguing the weight of the document, when the matter before this Bench is a matter of admissibility. Your Honours, the question arises as to whether or not the witnesses who are proposed by the Defence could in fact provide any information which would assist the Bench in the determination of the admissibility of this document. And Your Honours, it is submitted that they would not. Contrary to the submissions by the Defence that they are entitled to call the author of a document or the people related to chain of custody of the document before the question of admissibility is determined, the Appeals Chamber in Celebici, as quite rightly pointed out, that the decision in that case to admit a document did not in any way undermine the rights of the defendant to a fair trial or to confront the witness against him pursuant to Article 21, paragraph 4, subsection (e). The Trial Chamber - and this is at paragraph 22 -- or sorry, the Appeals Chamber, at paragraph 22, went on to say: "On the contrary, to require the attendance of the authors at this time stage of the proceedings would be, in the view of the bench, to acquire an extremely high standard for the purpose of a fair trial envisaged by Article 20, paragraph 1. Your Honour, the question for the Bench is a matter of admissibility of this document and therefore of its relevancy and probity and whether or not it is sufficiently reliable to meet the test of admissibility. Your Honour, should --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: So coming back to your sufficiently reliable, can you address us on that, the indicia that you want to rely on? Can you come to that at some time, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour. Can I just seek a clarification. Would you like me to argue on why we believe there is sufficient reliance in existence or what these -- what "sufficiently reliable" means?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: No, what it means. But we are looking at those documents -- at some time, please come back.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Okay. Then Your Honours, I would say that any of the -- any of the witnesses -- the evidence before this Chamber which makes this document, in the Prosecution's view, sufficiently reliable are a number of factors. They start from the fact that we are able to show that this document, although unsigned and unstamped, was not just found once or in one place in Bosnia but that a number of copies of it were found throughout Bosnia. We were able to show that numbers of the copies were found with different numberings on it. The evidence is on the record that contemporaneously a copy of the document was reproduced in a national magazine Slobodna Bosna. We were able to show that the persons who found the documents found them at different times, in different locations and they were different people, the most recent one having been found, as we said, by the international stabilisation force in Livno. We were able to produce a number of documents which testify that the document existed at the time the document purported to exist, that is, in December 1991. And in particular, I'd refer the Bench now to the Prosecution Exhibit P46, and those documents dealing 1 through to 10, which in every case there is a cross-reference to the instructions on the organisations of the activity of the Serbian people. And in a number of them, specifically, for example, Article 4 of the instructions is cross referred to, and it was the establishment of a Serbian municipality. And perhaps I can direct you directly to one of those, which is P46/8, that was the establishment of Donji Vakuf, and the cross-reference of that -- in the establishment of the municipality of Donji Vakuf is a cross-reference to Article 4 the Variant A/Variant B document, and the same applies for the decision on the establishment of the Serbian municipality of Tuzla, which I believe is P46/9. We've also been able to show that this was discussed by and within the SDS and indeed, as we said, by the president of the SDS, Mr. Karadzic. Your Honours, we believe that that evidence shows sufficient reliability that the document existed at the time we said it existed, that it was indeed widely distributed, and that it was indeed acted upon in a number of municipalities. Even if the witness who counsel for Milan Simic proposed were to come and testify, and based on his statement -- or his assertion in his letter, that is, that this document in fact originated from a number of JNA officers, that wouldn't go to disprove any of the reliable indicators we have put on the record. It wouldn't disprove that the document didn't exist at the time we said it existed. It wouldn't disprove that it was widely distributed to SDS offices. It wouldn't disprove that it was received by SDS offices. And it wouldn't disprove that the SDS party acted upon the instructions and set up a number of, for example, Serbian municipalities in accordance with the instructions. And Your Honours, it's our submission that all those factors go to an indicia of reliability where none of the witnesses can call into question that reliability. They could, as it appears Mr. Bjelica could, call into question the authorship. Of course, the Prosecution case is that that assertion is not reliable, nor does it fit with the evidence. Indeed, perhaps if Mr. Karadzic would like to come and testify, then -- as to his claim on the fiftieth transcript, that would be a great clarity as to the authorship. But Your Honours, that is in essence, is our submission. We have provided a reliable -- indicia of reliability. There is nothing that any of these witnesses who could come could do to challenge that reliability. It would simply be the Prosecution -- I mean, the Defence is entitled to raise their case as to -- they want to challenge this document. They want to bring other witnesses who will argue as to the weight that will be given to it, then they can do that. But they should do that in the Defence case in the natural course of the proceedings. And it should not be something that should go ahead at the decision -- at the time when the Bench is making determination simply on the admissibility of the -- of the evidence. Thank you.
